2.text: The shamans, however, combine in varying degrees all these categories

3.text: of Chukchee shamanism; that is, they converse with spirits, and make them

4.text: play various tricks before the spectators; then they make the spirits answer

5.text: the questions and give the necessary directions. If need be, they pronounce

6.text: incantations, and perform other magical acts. They also perform the magical

7.text: art in the treatment of various diseases.

8.text: PAY FOR SERVICES OF SHAMANS. — It goes without saying that Chukchee

9.text: shamans are paid for their services, and, besides, try to get for them as

10.text: much as possible. It is a common saying among them, that shamanistic

11.text: advice or treatment, when given gratuitously, amounts to nothing. The

12.text: “spirits” are too jealous of their power to spend it without pay, and they

13.text: even become angry for such doings, both with the shaman and with his

14.text: patients.¹ Even when, prompted by friendship or compassion, the shaman

15.text: does not ask for recompense, some symbolical remuneration must nevertheless

16.text: be given to him to make his treatment more effective. This, for the most

17.text: part, consists of a piece of sinew with a bead fastened to one end of it.

18.text: Usually the shamans and the “spirits” do not hesitate to express their

19.text: full opinion about this matter. Once, at a shamanistic séance given by
19.note: i don't think we will; §2.15 withdrawn: printed mark restored, read off the scan

20.text: Scratching-Woman in my presence, a woman from a neighboring camp asked

21.text: whether she might hope to have a child in the near future. The voice of

22.text: a keˊlᴇ who had already spoken a little before answered roughly, “I will not

23.text: speak without fresh meat.” The woman meekly promised to kill a reindeer.

24.text: “Then we shall see,” said the keˊlᴇ.

25.text: The substance and the amount of the payment vary, of course, in different

26.text: cases. Meat, thong, skins, garments, living reindeer, “alien food” of civilized

27.text: origin, — all are indiscriminately given by way of recompense for a shaman.

28.text: In the tale of the Scabby Shaman, Meeˊmhɪn pays for the services of the

29.text: shaman with a large reindeer-herd of his possession,² but I much doubt whether

30.text: cases like that happen in actual life. A reindeer-breeder of the Omolon told

31.text: me, however, that he paid a Lamut shaman who cured him of a severe

32.text: illness three large bucks and some skins besides. Sometimes a man cured by

33.text: a shaman has to give him in payment something that from personal motives

34.text: he prizes exeedingly high; for instance, his own reindeer-team. This may be

35.text: compared with a similar sacrifice to the “spirits.”³ I have never met shamans,

36.text: however, who could be said to live solely on the profits of their art: it had

37.text: only been to them a source of additional income.

38.text: PREPARATION FOR PERFORMANCE. — As said before, preparation for each

39.text: shamanistic performance is similar to the preparatory period of inspiration

40.text: which is so painful to the novice shaman as to be considered almost a peculiar

41.text: kind of sickness. In conformity to this, most of the shamans show marked
